Title: Automatic Retry for Failed Subscription Payments — ArraySubs

Highlights:
When a renewal fails, the most dangerous response is also the easiest to automate: keep submitting the same charge until something changes. That can recover a temporary decline, but it can also repeat an impossible payment, conflict with a gateway-owned recovery flow, or charge an order that already succeeded remotely.

Good automatic retry does not repeat every failed charge on a fixed loop. It identifies who owns collection, separates retryable failures from customer-action and stop conditions, verifies that the order was not already paid, spaces a limited number of attempts inside the grace window, communicates clearly, and reconciles the order, subscription, gateway, and access state after recovery.
...
An initial attempt is the first collection attempt for a renewal that has become due. An automatic retry is a later system-triggered attempt against that same unresolved obligation. Reconciliation means making the gateway payment, WooCommerce renewal order, subscription status, next renewal date, scheduled jobs, and customer access agree with the verified outcome.
...
Automatic retry helps when the cause may resolve without changing the payment context. A temporary processing problem or permitted insufficient-funds decline may succeed later. WooCommerce Subscriptions has its own optional failed-payment retry engine. Its current documentation describes rule-based intervals, emails, order statuses, and subscription statuses, with five default rules across seven days. Title: WooCommerce Subscription Card Expired? Fix (2026)
URL: https://wptechhouse.com/fix/woocommerce-subscription-card-expired/
Published: 2026-07-16T01:05:13.000Z
Author: John O'Keane, David Zhang
Highlights:
A renewal was declined, the subscription is drifting toward On hold, and nobody raised a hand. Almost always the saved card expired or was replaced, and the off-session charge had nothing valid to bill. Here's how to confirm it and get the customer paying again.
...
The most common cause is that the stored card expired or was reissued, so the off-session renewal charge was declined — typically with an `expired_card` or `card_declined` code at the gateway. WooCommerce Subscriptions then works through its failed-payment retry rules before giving up and putting the subscription On hold. The fix is to get the customer to add a new card, then process the renewal manually.
...
Renewals are off-session: nobody is at the checkout. WooCommerce asks the gateway to charge a saved token, the gateway looks at the card behind that token, sees an expiry date in the past (or a card the issuer has since replaced), and declines. No customer is present to be told, so the only trace is a failed renewal order, a gateway decline code, and — if retries are enabled — a queue of scheduled retry attempts.
...
1. The saved card has passed its expiry date The gateway shows the declined renewal with an expired-card decline code, and the card's expiry month/year on the subscription is in the past. The plainest version of the problem.
2. The issuer replaced the card, so the old token no longer works The card hasn't technically expired, but the charge is still declined — the customer was reissued a card after loss, fraud or a bank migration, and the stored token points at the dead one.
3. The retry system is still running, so it looks like nothing is wrong yet The renewal order is Pending or Failed, the subscription is On hold, and there are scheduled retry actions queued. The decline already happened; the store is just not finished admitting it.
4. Retries are disabled, so a single decline ends the subscription immediately Renewal fails once and the subscription goes straight to On hold with no second attempt — check whether automatic retry is switched on at all in the Subscriptions settings.
5. The retry emails are not reaching the customer Retries ran, the subscription is On hold, and the customer swears they were never told. The decline is real but the recovery path is broken — that's a mail-delivery problem sitting on top of a card problem.
6. Automatic card updating is off or unsupported for that card Every expiry becomes a manual fire drill. Some gateways can pull reissued card details from the card networks automatically; if that feature is off, or the card brand isn't covered, every renewal after an expiry fails.
...
- Open the failed renewal order and read the order notes — they usually carry the gateway's decline reason verbatim. An expired-card or declined code there confirms cause 1 or 2 and you can stop looking at your store.
- Cross-check in the gateway dashboard. Find the declined charge and read the decline code. If the gateway never received a charge attempt at all, this isn't an expired card — it's a renewal that never fired, which is a different fault.
- Check `WooCommerce → Status → Scheduled Actions` for retry actions against this subscription. Pending retries mean the retry rules are still walking; failed or complete ones mean the store has already given up.
- Check `WooCommerce → Settings → Subscriptions` and confirm automatic retry of failed payments is enabled. If it isn't, one bad card equals one lost customer with no second chance (cause 4).
- Get a new card on the subscription, then charge it. The customer can update it themselves from `My Account → Subscriptions` using the change-payment-method link in the renewal email. Once a valid card is saved, process the outstanding renewal and the subscription reactivates.
...

Most guides on perishable shipping focus on insulation, gel packs and carrier selection. Those matter. But the highest-risk moment for spoilage isn’t in transit — it’s when a customer places an order on Friday afternoon and the package sits in a warehouse over the weekend before the courier collects on Monday.

The best Shopify delivery date picker for perishable goods prevents that order from happening in the first place.

Weekend and non-shipping day blocking. Perishable products can’t survive two days without climate control. Flare blocks weekend delivery dates and any non-shipping days from the customer calendar automatically. A customer shopping on Thursday evening doesn’t see Friday delivery if your cut-off has passed — and doesn’t see Saturday or Sunday at all. The next available date is Monday or Tuesday, depending on your carrier’s transit time from their zone.

Carrier cut-off enforcement. Your cold chain courier collects at 2pm. An order placed at 3pm can’t make that collection. Without cut-off rules, Shopify shows tomorrow’s delivery — but the product won’t ship until the day after. For chilled goods with a 48-hour shelf window, that extra day is the difference between fresh delivery and a spoilage complaint. Flare applies cut-off times by shipping method and zone, so customers always see dates that reflect your actual dispatch schedule.

Transit time rules by postcode zone. A customer in a neighbouring city might receive next-day delivery. A customer 300 miles away needs two-day express. Flare calculates the delivery date from the customer’s postcode, your carrier’s transit time for that zone, and the product’s lead time — so the date shown is the date the product actually arrives, not a generic “3–5 business days” range that risks spoilage at the far end.

## What it is and how to set it up on your EPoS System.

Managing waste is an essential way of controlling costs, no more so than now when we are facing a rise in national insurance contributions, business rates and national minimum wage. Typically, you would like to see an optimal amount of products in your shop to meet demand. But as we all know, a change in the weather, a road closure or any other factors you may not have considered at the time of production, could mean excess products left over at the end of the day. This waste not only affects your bottom line but incurs additional costs to dispose of and has an environmental impact too.

Sending it off to local charities and food banks not only reduces your disposal costs but also benefits the local community. And now you can generate additional income on some of your surplus products by making it available on the Too Good To Go platform. Users can purchase “Surprise Bags” filled with unsold goods at a discounted price. This also has an additional benefit as you can potentially reach new customers, especially customers who are interested in sustainable shopping.

But how do you operate this through your EPoS system ? Firstly, you must still treat these products as waste. With systems like sales-based ordering or if you are looking at your product sales reports, your production planning will be skewed by the products you have sold in your Surprise Bags and you will be producing more products to satisfy your To Good To Go customers, therefore creating more waste!.

The Surprise Bags should be set up in your EPoS system as a separate product of a fixed value (including VAT), and the items in the Surprise bags should be recorded as waste.

We found that our customers wanted to monitor the products going into the Surprise bags, so we created a brand-new Waste Type for this purpose. Our customers can easily see the breakdown of the different types of waste (Unsold Waste, Damaged Waste, Sample Waste, To Good To Go Waste) which are all included in the % waste calculations of the reports.

With our ingredient and allergen printing module (which can be linked to your production systems i.e Cybake and FoodLogiK), tickets can be printed from the EPoS system containing the ingredients and allergen information on the receipt printers and stapled or stuck to the Surprise Bags.
